general.temas: Diplomacy and international cooperation, technological development and space missions are recurring themes. Environmental protection and the climate also feature. COVID-19 coverage is especially prominent in Xinhua.
general.motivo_crispacion: Tensions center on protests in the United States against attacks on Iran, technology restrictions between Washington and Beijing, and Chinese criticism of talks between Japan and the Philippines. Huawei’s conviction in the United States and investigations into Chinese officials also feature prominently. Stories about diplomatic cooperation, culture and space exploration offer a calmer counterpoint. The headlines date from different periods, so the score reflects the collection as a whole rather than a single verifiable day.

Diario del Pueblo.resumen:
- World Environment Day is the focus of several stories on ecological protection, sustainable development and improvements to rural areas, linked to Xi Jinping.
- The front page covers the summer harvest and announces a national agricultural census for 2026.
- New regulations on military facilities and Party discipline are introduced, along with an inspection of the enforcement of the energy conservation law.
- Ding Xuexiang oversees preparations in Shanxi to ensure the security and fairness of the university entrance exam.
- Other highlights include dialogue between China and the United States, traditional Longjing tea production and a review of Xi’s activities in May 2025.
Diario del Pueblo.motivo_populismo: The headlines are mostly institutional, although they use emotive expressions such as “caring for mountains and rivers” and “winning the heart of the world”; there is no apparent confrontation between the people and the elites.
Diario del Pueblo.sesgo: The selection and wording give favorable prominence to Xi Jinping and the actions of the Party and the government. An institutional perspective predominates, with little representation of independent or critical viewpoints.

Xinhua.resumen:
- COVID-19 stories predominate, covering the reopening of businesses, vaccination and advice for vulnerable people.
- Experts respond to questions about data on asymptomatic infections, and the BQ.1 variant is discussed.
- A video presents the changes in China, while another story highlights three astronauts’ years of preparation.
- Speeches and diplomatic activities by Xi Jinping are announced, including one on biodiversity.
- The front page also covers tighter financial oversight and the arrival of a cold wave.
Xinhua.motivo_populismo: The headlines are mostly informative; some use questions and an emotive tone, such as the one highlighting the astronauts’ years of preparation.
Xinhua.sesgo: The selection gives extensive space to public health measures and the authorities, with an approach favorable to institutional action. It also presents changes in China and the astronauts’ preparation in positive terms.

Global Times.resumen:
- Analysts warn that the FCC’s plan to exclude Chinese laboratories could disrupt supply chains and raise costs.
- A Chinese expert criticizes Philippine statements on delimitation with Japan; another headline addresses the Tokyo trial and the Yasukuni Shrine.
- Protests in the United States after a month of attacks on Iran and the writings of a suspect in a Washington shooting are highlighted.
- China announces a new railway timetable, prepares a lunar mission and presents a favorable outlook for its artificial intelligence.
- The front page also covers South Africa, multilateralism, visits from Taiwan and a sex education proposal in China.
Global Times.motivo_populismo: Although several headlines are informative, expressions such as “notorious,” “ulterior purposes” and “more chaos” add a negative and alarmist tone.
Global Times.sesgo: The selection and wording show an approach favorable to China, highlighting its advances and international role while presenting the actions of the United States, Japan and the Philippines critically.

CGTN.resumen:
- Chinese envoys step up their peace efforts in the Middle East and the Horn of Africa.
- Experts give a positive assessment of a trilateral meeting between China, Russia and the United States.
- China holds cooperation talks with Switzerland, Vietnam and ASEAN.
- A magnitude 5.6 earthquake shakes northwestern China; an AI platform for Earth system research is also announced.
- The front page covers Chinese culture, Shenzhen’s development, anxiety and Trump’s criticism of US cities.
CGTN.motivo_populismo: Informative language predominates, although “the making of a miracle” for Shenzhen and Trump’s description of US cities as “disgraceful” introduce value-laden expressions.
CGTN.sesgo: The selection highlights China’s diplomatic role and advances, generally from a favorable perspective. It also includes a comparison favorable to China attributed to Trump.

South China Morning Post.resumen:
- BYD is considering building an electric vehicle plant in Brazil, while three states seek to attract it.
- A US jury finds Huawei guilty on 10 of 12 charges; Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia could deepen divisions in the United States over chip restrictions on China.
- Chinese American residents of Texas hope for changes to property ownership restrictions; in China, Shanghai’s Communist Party chief and a senior science official are under investigation.
- The front page covers the reception of Japan’s prime minister in China, the planned debut of a Chinese naval training aircraft and a new designation for a US nuclear bomb.
- A new union brings together Asian mathematicians; a study questions possible biases in Chinese climate records, and the Tiangong station will welcome a Pakistani astronaut.
South China Morning Post.motivo_populismo: The headlines are mostly informative, although expressions such as “the hope of 250 million,” “the brightest minds” and the rivalry between states add emotional emphasis and drama.
South China Morning Post.sesgo: The selection prioritizes China’s relations with the United States and other countries, particularly in technology, security and diplomacy. It combines stories about official investigations and trade disputes with scientific advances and regional cooperation.

opiniones.comunista:
I see the same class question in environmental protection, food production and the contest between Brazilian states over a possible BYD electric vehicle factory: who decides where investment goes, and who receives its rewards?

I welcome the inspection of compliance with the energy conservation law and the preparation of a new agricultural census in China. But measuring and monitoring are not enough: the data must be used to direct public resources toward those who work the land and to protect the environment on which their lives depend.

In Brazil, competing to attract capital should not mean handing a major investor the power to set the terms of development. I support decent jobs, public services and collective ownership wherever public investment sustains production. The ecological transition will be just when the working class can govern it, not merely carry it out.
opiniones.anarquista:
The front pages speak of protecting nature and securing harvests. I share those priorities, but I doubt they can be addressed through orders handed down from above. Those who work the land and live alongside rivers need the power to make decisions about them, organize freely and share knowledge and resources without being subordinated to officials or powerful interests.

I also read about a proposal to incorporate comprehensive sex education into basic education. I see it as an opportunity to advocate education that gives people the tools to make decisions about their own bodies, not to impose obedience. Individual freedom needs mutual support: accessible information, a willingness to listen and communities capable of caring for themselves without being placed under anyone’s guardianship. Neither the state nor political parties should claim a monopoly over those decisions; a freer society is built through cooperation among equals.
opiniones.liberal:
The news about environmental protection in China reminds me that prosperity and nature need not be in conflict. But protecting rivers and fields requires more than official plans: clear rules, secure property rights and accountability for polluters. If those responsible bear the costs of the damage, entrepreneurs and farmers have incentives to conserve resources and seek solutions.

I am also concerned about the US plan to exclude Chinese electronics testing laboratories. Raising barriers to trade can make products more expensive and disrupt supply chains, as the analysts quoted warn. I prefer open competition to political protection for favored companies. A limited state should enforce contracts and protect rights, not direct every economic decision. And with low taxes, people retain more freedom and more responsibility to decide how to invest, work and live.
opiniones.extrema_derecha:
I do not see sovereignty as a diplomatic slogan, but as a nation’s ability to feed itself, defend itself and pass on its culture. That is why I believe China is right to prioritize grain production and its military facilities: a country that depends on others to meet its essential needs can hardly decide its future freely.

I also welcome the protection of crafts such as traditional Longjing tea production. Traditions are not ornaments for tourists; they are inherited knowledge and bonds that deserve to endure. But I distrust the official press when it presents every initiative as proof of the wisdom of those in power. National discipline requires capable authorities and informed citizens, not propaganda. Security and care for the land must be measured by their results, not by the praise they receive from those in power.
opiniones.centro:
I see in the front pages a tension that defines our time: we need international cooperation, but also rules that protect our communities. Dialogue between China and the United States deserves support, even when there are serious disagreements. The alternative to negotiation is not resolve, but the risk that each country will confuse security with isolation. Before imposing restrictions on Chinese laboratories, Washington should assess the specific risks and the costs to supply chains.

I also welcome the prominent place given to environmental protection. Turning that priority into lasting results requires institutions capable of checking compliance with the law, listening to communities and correcting mistakes. Markets can drive the transition, but they are no substitute for public regulations or support for those who must bear its costs. I prefer gradual, verifiable reforms to grandiose promises.
